title: slo-driven-priority-eviction-workshop-notes
summary: Notes from a cross-functional architecture workshop focused on designing an SLO-driven request prioritization and eviction system for the serving runtime. Goal: produce a concrete, deployable design that balances customer SLOs, cost, and fairness under overload.
agenda: Recap of overload scenarios observed in Feb
Walk through simulation results from Kenji
Discuss eviction granularity and preemption mechanics
notes:
Background: Multiple customer incidents in Feb showed tail-latency spikes when capacity hit because of high prefix reuse in cache-heavy workloads + large long-form generations. Current fallback (serve lower-capacity model) causes significant quality regressions for high-SLA customers. Workshop reframed the problem: instead of coarse fallbacks, implement SLO-driven prioritization and deterministic eviction of low-value requests under overload.

Simulation summary (Kenji): ran 3 traffic mixes over historical traces (chatty short sessions, long-form bursts, embedding-heavy batch jobs). Key results: prioritization by SLO bucket with small preemption budget improved p99 latency for high-tier customers by ~35% while increasing average overall latency by ~8%. Pure FIFO eviction reduced overall fairness and caused per-tenant starvation.

Priority model discussed: define three runtime buckets: guaranteed (reserved tokens/capacity for enterprise customers with Dedicated/Dedicated+), best-effort with soft-SLOs, and background (non-interactive batch jobs like nightly embeddings). Requests carry a priority vector derived from (customer_tier, route_slo, request_cost_estimate). The runtime will allocate ephemeral soft-reservations at batch creation time and attach a preemption token that allows higher-priority requests to evict queued lower-priority batches when necessary.

Eviction granularity: debate between batch-level eviction (evict whole request/batch) vs. token-level preemption (stop in-progress generation). Consensus: start with batch-level preemption for simplicity and safety (stop queued batches and fail fast), and prototype token-level preemption only for small, idempotent streaming requests where partial output is acceptable. Token-level preemption adds KV cache rollback complexity and will be scoped to phase 2.

Preemption semantics and customer impact: preempted requests should receive clear error codes and a short Retry-After header. For hosted-api, product should present a graceful UX. For Dedicated customers with contractual SLAs, preemption should be opt-in at contract level; Dedicated pools will prefer capacity isolation instead.

Fairness concerns: implement per-tenant ingress watermarks to prevent a single tenant from monopolizing background buckets. Also add decaying soft-quota based on recent usage to avoid starvation of mid-tier customers.

Caching interaction: eviction of queued batches must not invalidate shared KV caches aggressively. Proposed policy: mark cache entries as "no-evict-on-preempt" for a short TTL if they are heavily reused in the last N minutes; otherwise allow natural eviction. This avoids a preempt->cache-evict spiral.

Telemetry/instrumentation: must add the following metrics and traces so we can validate effects in canary: priority_bucket_latency_histogram (p50/ p90/ p99), preempt_count_by_bucket, preempt_reason_tags, per-tenant_bg_usage, preemption_latency_penalty, cache_no_evict_hits. Logging should correlate request_id, tenant_id, assigned_priority, and eviction_decision_id.

Rollout plan: 3-phase rollout. Phase 0: simulate prioritization in the scheduler (no enforcement) and surface simulated outcomes in dashboards for 2 weeks. Phase 1 (canary): enforce prioritization on 5% of host clusters; batch-level preemption enabled for background bucket only. Phase 2: enlarge canary to 30% with enterprise opt-in behavior for Dedicated customers. Phase 3: global rollout with token-preemption prototype toggles if telemetry supports.

Risks noted: incorrect cost-accounting on preempted work could overcharge customers (need to mark preempt billing as 0-cost for background). Cache churn if preemption spikes. UX confusion for customers seeing more 429s.

Operational playbooks: SRE to add a runbook for high preempt rates: thresholds -> alert -> temporary global softening of priorities -> investigate tenant causing surge.
decisions: Adopt SLO-driven priority buckets (guaranteed, best-effort, background) as canonical model
Implement batch-level preemption for phase 1; token-level preemption deferred to phase 2 exploration
Reserved capacity (Dedicated) will default to "guaranteed" and require contract opt-out to participate in preemption
Introduce per-tenant ingress watermarks and decaying soft-quotas to maintain fairness
Telemetry metric set agreed (see instrumentation notes) and required before canary enforcement

open_questions: What exact SLA/contract language is required to make Dedicated customers opt into preemption? (product/legal)
Should the system prefer evicting the oldest queued request or the lowest cost-estimate request when choosing victims?
How to represent partial progress for streaming responses if token-level preemption is added?
What safe default Retry-After values should we set for various buckets?
Do we need a separate billing meter for preempted work and should that be visible in console usage reports?
